claim: Sexual selection is generally predicted to act more strongly on males than on females.
source: Sexual selection is generally predicted to act more strongly on males than on females.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific prediction in sexual selection theory.

claim: The Darwin-Bateman paradigm predicts that sexual selection should act more strongly on males than on females in hermaphrodites.
source: The Darwin-Bateman paradigm predicts that this should also hold for hermaphrodites.
evidence: This extends the Darwin-Bateman paradigm to hermaphrodites based on theoretical predictions.

claim: Male sexual selection gradients are consistently positive in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Our results show that male sexual selection gradients are consistently positive.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: An individual's female mating success negatively affects its own male reproductive success in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: However, an individual's female mating success seems to negatively affect its own male reproductive success, an effect that only becomes visible several weeks into the experiment
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data showing cross-sex effects.

claim: The time frame is crucial for the quantification and interpretation of sexual selection measures.
source: highlighting that the time frame is crucial for the quantification and interpretation of sexual selection measures, an insight that applies to any iteroparous mating system.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the temporal analysis of sexual selection gradients in the study.

claim: Darwin defined sexual selection as selection on traits that affect mating success.
source: Darwin defined sexual selection as selection on traits that affect mating success (Darwin, 1871).
evidence: This is a historical definition attributed to Darwin with citation.

claim: Sexual selection acts not only prior to mating (pre-copulatory) but also after mating (post-copulatory).
source: In recent decades, this definition has been refined, most notable due to the realisation that sexual selection does not only act prior to mating – referred to as pre-copulatory sexual selection (Darwin's focus) - but also after mating - post-copulatory sexual selection (e.g., Parker, 1970; Eberhard, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Parker (1970) and Eberhard (1996).

claim: Simultaneous hermaphrodites are under influence of the same selective pressures as species with separate sexes.
source: These sexual selection processes are often measured, but with a strong bias towards species with separate sexes, even though simultaneous hermaphrodites are under influence of the same selective pressures (Charnov, 1979; Nakadera and Koene, 2013; Pélissié et al., 2012; Schärer and Pen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Bateman (1948) showed that the factors that limit reproductive success for males and females are different.
source: One, now classical, study on Drosophila melanogaster by Bateman (1948) sparked the pivotal insight that the factors that limit reproductive success for males and females are different.
evidence: This is a historical finding attributed to Bateman with citation.

claim: Anisogamy results in a clear difference in the cost of producing male and female gametes.
source: Due to anisogamy, for which sexual selection has been an important driving force (reviewed in Parker and Birkhead, 2013), a clear difference is found in the cost of producing male and female gametes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review by Parker and Birkhead (2013).

claim: Sperm production is generally not a limiting factor for males.
source: As a consequence, sperm production is generally not a limiting factor for males, so the number of fathered offspring (male reproductive success, RSm; Bateman, 1948) depends directly on the number of mates the male can inseminate.
evidence: This is a consequence of anisogamy and the Darwin-Bateman paradigm, supported by citation.

claim: Egg production is highly dependent on available resources and limits the number of offspring females can produce.
source: In contrast, egg production is highly dependent on available resources and therefore limits the number of offspring the female can produce (i.e., female reproductive success, RSf; Bateman, 1948).
evidence: This is a consequence of anisogamy and the Darwin-Bateman paradigm, supported by citation.

claim: Bateman's experiment has been criticized based on experimental design, data collection, and repeatability.
source: Even though Bateman's experiment has been criticized based on experimental design as well as data collection and actual repeatability (e.g., Gowaty et al., 2012; Gowaty et al., 2013), the basics of the Darwin-Bateman paradigm still hold (e.g., Janicke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to critical papers and a defense of the paradigm.

claim: The basics of the Darwin-Bateman paradigm still hold despite criticisms.
source: Even though Bateman's experiment has been criticized based on experimental design as well as data collection and actual repeatability (e.g., Gowaty et al., 2012; Gowaty et al., 2013), the basics of the Darwin-Bateman paradigm still hold (e.g., Janicke et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janicke et al. (2016).

claim: The sexual selection gradient (Bateman gradient) looks at the linear relationship between mating success and reproductive success.
source: One insightful measure that has emerged is the sexual selection gradient (also referred to as Bateman gradient), which looks at the linear relationship between mating success and reproductive success (β; e.g., Arnold and Duvall, 1994; Anthes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citations.

claim: In simultaneous hermaphrodites, mating success in the male role can affect the individual's male reproductive success and female reproductive success.
source: Hence, besides that mating success in the male role can affect the individual's male reproductive success, it can also directly affect its female reproductive success and vice versa.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of hermaphroditism and is explained in the text.

claim: Cross-sex effects in hermaphrodites are interactions between the sexual functions of the individual.
source: These interactions between the sexual functions of the individual are referred to as cross-sex effects (βmf and βfm; Anthes et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a definition with citation to Anthes et al. (2010).

claim: It is possible to quantify sexual selection in simultaneous hermaphrodites.
source: As illustrated by several recent studies, it is possible to quantify sexual selection in simultaneous hermaphrodites (Ophryotrocha diadema: Lorenzi and Sella, 2008; Biomphalaria glabrata: Anthes et al., 2010; Physa acuta: Pélissié et al., 2012; Macrostomum lignano: Marie-Orleach et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Most sexual selection gradient studies on separate sexed species and hermaphrodites used a very restricted time window (days).
source: Like in most of the sexual selection gradient studies on separate sexed species, these studies used a very restricted time window (days) within which the strength of sexual selection was estimated.
evidence: This is an observation about the methodology of previous studies.

claim: Many species are long-lived, mate many times, and can store and use sperm for extended periods.
source: However, many species are long-lived, mate many times and can store and use sperm for extended periods (e.g., Nakadera and Koene, 2013; Nakadera et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The relationship between mating success and reproductive success can be expected to change over time.
source: Therefore, the relationship between mating success and reproductive success can be expected to change over time, especially when considering that sperm storage becomes important as soon as individuals are no longer virgin, meaning that the degree to which mating success translated into reproductive success might change (Baena and Macías-Ordóñez, 2012; Wacker et al., 2014; Anthes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a prediction based on biological reasoning and supported by citations.

claim: The experiment quantified mating success and reproductive success in Lymnaea stagnalis over an eight week period.
source: Here, we present an experiment in which we quantify mating success and reproductive success, using the great pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis, over an eight week period that represents roughly a quarter of its reproductive life in nature.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: A total of 7888 matings were observed during the experiment.
source: During the whole experiment, a total of 7888 matings were observed in the first two treatments (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: An estimated 343,745 eggs were produced during the experiment.
source: Of the estimated 343,745 eggs that were produced, 1102 were genotyped (excluding eggs from the selfing No partner treatment).
evidence: This is a quantification from the experimental data.

claim: Overall survival during the experiment was 87.8%.
source: Overall survival during the whole experiment was 87.8%, which is within the common range for this species in our experience, and did not differ between the treatment groups (χ22 = 1.303, p = 0.521).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experiment with statistical analysis.

claim: Survival did not differ between treatment groups.
source: Overall survival during the whole experiment was 87.8%, which is within the common range for this species in our experience, and did not differ between the treatment groups (χ22 = 1.303, p = 0.521).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The opportunity for selection values (Im and If) are larger for the male role than the female role.
source: Comparison of the opportunity for selection values between the male and female role (Im and If) shows that these values are larger for the male role (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in figures.

claim: The opportunity for selection values decreased over the course of the experiment.
source: In addition, these values decreased over the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal analysis of the data.

claim: The opportunity for sexual selection values (Ism and Isf) are much lower than the opportunity for selection values and show a similar decreasing trend.
source: The much lower values for the opportunity for sexual selection (Ism and Isf) reveal a similar trend (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis shown in figures.

claim: The factor relative MSm has a significant effect on relative RSm.
source: This analysis revealed a significant effect for the factor relative MSm on relative RSm (F1, 145.5 = 7.872; p = 0.0057)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The male sexual selection gradient (βmm) is positive and does not change over time.
source: This indicates that the male sexual selection gradient, βmm, is positive and does not change over time, as is also clearly reflected in the regression lines (Figure 2; see β-values in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, the slopes' confidence intervals in Figure 2—source data 2, and slope comparisons between weeks in Figure 2—source data 3)
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis and visualization of the data.

claim: Continued mating in the male role assures continuous male reproductive success beyond the first week.
source: revealing that continued mating in the male role assures continuous male reproductive success beyond the first week.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the positive male sexual selection gradient over time.

claim: The factor relative MSf has a significant effect on relative RSm.
source: When looking at the cross-sex effect βmf in this model, the factor relative MSf had a significant effect on relative RSm (F1, 145.7 = 29.956; p = 0.0001)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There is a significant positive relationship between the number of male matings and female reproductive success in the first week.
source: which is due to the significant positive relationship between the number of male matings and female reproductive success in the first week, as reflected by the significance of the interaction term Week*relative MSf (F7, 136.1 = 4.159; p = 0.0004); an effect that disappeared afterwards (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis with temporal dynamics.

claim: There is a significant relationship between female mating success and female reproductive success.
source: From the female perspective, running the same model with relative RSf as dependent variable, for the female role (βff), a significant relationship between female mating success and female reproductive success is found (F1, 140.6 = 5.101; p = 0.0255)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The relationship between female mating success and female reproductive success seems to be caused by negative trend lines in the last three weeks of the experiment.
source: which seems to be caused by the negative trend lines found in the last three weeks of the experiment (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in figures.

claim: Relative MSm has a significant effect on relative RSf.
source: For the cross sex effect βfm the model revealed a significant effect of relative MSm on relative RSf (F1, 140,5 = 13.523; p = 0.0003)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The effect of relative MSm on relative RSf seems due to the initial positive correlation in Week 1 and 2.
source: which seem due to the initial positive correlation (in Week 1 and 2; Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), even though the interaction term Week*relative MSm was not significant.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in figures.

claim: A more female biased mating rate can negatively affect male reproductive success.
source: One crucial difference to note between the two analytical approaches is that a more female biased mating rate (i.e., higher PC1 values) can negatively affect male reproductive success (negative slope, βmPC1), which is not seen in the regression analysis between relative MSf and relative RSm.
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis of the data.

claim: A more female biased mating rate may negatively affect the individual's female reproductive success.
source: Similar negative trend lines are seen for βfPC1 and βff, confirming that a more female biased mating rate may also negatively affect the individual's female reproductive success (in terms of offspring number, but see below).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis of the data.

claim: There is no significant correlation between male and female mating success in the Multiple partner treatment.
source: When looking at the relationship between male and female mating success (respectively, MSm and MSf) in the Multiple partner treatment, no significant correlation emerges (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Animals keep mating as male and female throughout the experiment.
source: The statistical significance of the factor Week simply reflects the cumulative nature of these data and reveals that animals keep mating as male and female throughout the experiment, as also illustrated in Figure 4.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis and visualization.

claim: Mean cumulative mating success at Week 2 averaged around 3 matings for each sexual role.
source: For example, mean cumulative mating success at Week 2 averaged around 3 and at Week 8 around 12 matings for each sexual role.
evidence: This is a quantification from the experimental data.

claim: Mean cumulative mating success at Week 8 averaged around 12 matings for each sexual role.
source: For example, mean cumulative mating success at Week 2 averaged around 3 and at Week 8 around 12 matings for each sexual role.
evidence: This is a quantification from the experimental data.

claim: There was a slight correlation between male and female reproductive success in Week 2.
source: While there was a slight correlation in Week 2 (R = 0.41, N = 24, p = 0.046; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; which might explain the positive relationship between MSm and RSf in the first two weeks, see above)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The correlation between male and female reproductive success was absent throughout the rest of the experiment after Week 2.
source: this relationship was absent throughout the rest of the experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Animals keep obtaining male and female reproductive success over the course of the experiment.
source: Again, the statistical significance of the factor Week reflects the cumulative nature of these data and reveals that animals keep obtaining male and female reproductive success over the course of the experiment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical analysis.

claim: Mean reproductive success at Week 2 was higher for the female than the male role.
source: For example, mean reproductive success at Week 2 was higher for the female than the male role, but these means lie much closer together at Week 8, around 2000 eggs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantification from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Mean reproductive success at Week 8 was around 2000 eggs for both male and female roles.
source: For example, mean reproductive success at Week 2 was higher for the female than the male role, but these means lie much closer together at Week 8, around 2000 eggs (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantification from the experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Male and female reproductive success are not equal because selfing occurs at the start of the experiment, which only contributes to RSf.
source: The reason for male and female reproductive success not being equal is found in the fact that selfing occurs at the start of the experiment, which only contributes to RSf.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern in the data.

claim: There was no difference in body size (shell length and body weight) between the focals of the different treatments.
source: There was no difference in body size (shell length: ANOVA: F2, 69 = 2.385, p = 0.100; body weight: ANOVA: F2, 61 = 1.441, p = 0.245) between the focals of the different treatments.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was no difference in number of eggs between the masses produced by the focals of the different treatments at the end of the experiment.
source: Also, we found no difference in number of eggs between the masses produced by the focals of the different treatments at the end of the experiment (ANOVA: F2, 63 = 0.155, p = 0.857).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The overall proportion of hatching success and development differed between the treatments.
source: The overall proportion of hatching success and development scored after 14 days differed between the treatments (χ22 = 473.245, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: In the Multiple partners treatment significantly more offspring had reached hatching than in the No partner treatment.
source: Using nonparametric multiple comparisons, we found that in the Multiple partners treatment significantly more offspring had reached hatching than in the No partner treatment (Wilcoxon: Z = −2.609, p = 0.009)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The Single partner treatment did not differ significantly from either the Multiple partners or No partner treatment in hatching success.
source: while the Single partner treatment did not differ significantly from either treatment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in a figure.

claim: The Single partner and No partner treatments differ significantly from each other in the proportion of undeveloped offspring.
source: When looking at the proportion of undeveloped offspring, the Single partner and No partner treatments differ significantly from each other (Wilcoxon: Z = 2.060, p = 0.039)
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The difference between the Multiple partners and No partner treatment in undeveloped offspring shows a trend.
source: while the difference between the Multiple partners and No partner treatment shows a trend (Wilcoxon: Z = 1.714, p = 0.086; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis shown in a figure.

claim: This is the first study to look in detail at the effect of repeated mating on reproductive success over time in a simultaneous hermaphrodite.
source: The study that we present here is the first to look in detail at the effect of repeated mating on reproductive success over time in a simultaneous hermaphrodite.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The potential gain in reproductive success is consistently positive via the male function in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Firstly, we showed that the potential gain in reproductive success is consistently positive via the male function.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: The existence of cross-sex effects was supported by the sexual selection gradients.
source: Secondly, the existence of cross-sex effects was supported by the sexual selection gradients, emphasizing that their effects are important in the long run.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Sexual selection gradients change over time in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Thirdly, our data clearly showed that sexual selection gradients change over time, which is important for the interpretation of these values.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Repeated mating was beneficial for the development of offspring in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Fourthly, we showed that in this pond snail, repeated mating was beneficial for the development of offspring.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis mates unilateral, without any conditional role alternation.
source: Finally, our data confirmed that the investigated hermaphrodite mates unilateral, without any conditional role alternation.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: In short-term experiments, one can separate pre- from post-copulatory components of sexual selection by looking at the residual variance in reproductive success.
source: In short-term experiments, and (imposed) semelparous situations, one can separate pre- from post-copulatory components of sexual selection by looking at the residual variance in reproductive success, i.e. the variance not explained by mating success (this residual can be explained by post-copulatory processes: Rose et al., 2013a, 2013b; Pélissié et al., 2014; Janicke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations.

claim: Separating pre- from post-copulatory components of sexual selection is no longer straight-forward in longer running experiments where everyone has mated repeatedly and sperm is stored.
source: This is no longer straight-forward in a dataset from a longer running experiment where everyone has mated repeatedly with everyone else and sperm from those previous matings is still in storage.
evidence: This is a methodological insight from the study.

claim: At the end of the experiment 19% to 52% of the variance in reproductive success is explained by mating success.
source: So, even though our data show that at the end of the experiment 19% to 52% of the variance in reproductive success (RS) is explained by mating success (MS; which is essentially pre-copulatory)
evidence: This is a quantification from the data analysis.

claim: Post-copulatory processes such as sperm storage and sperm competition have had time to act on reproductive success in the long-term experiment.
source: post-copulatory processes, such as sperm storage and sperm competition, have had time to act on reproductive success (and are thus partially included).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics in the experiment.

claim: Age becomes a confounding factor in long-term experiments and cannot be fully excluded.
source: For example, age now becomes a confounding factor and cannot be fully excluded.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration from the study.

claim: These considerations apply to any species that mates multiple times over an extended reproductive period and stores sperm before producing eggs.
source: These considerations are of biologically relevance because they apply to any species, separate sexed or hermaphroditic, that mates multiple times over an extended reproductive period and stores sperm before producing eggs.
evidence: This is a generalization of the study's implications.

claim: Pélissié et al. (2014) and Turnell and Shaw (2015) took mating order into account in their studies.
source: The only studies that have been able to deal with this issue partly (though not the factor age), so far, are the ones by Pélissié et al. (2014) and Turnell and Shaw (2015). They achieved this by taking mating order into account, which was facilitated by the short duration of their experiments
evidence: This is a citation to previous methodological approaches.

claim: The findings of Pélissié et al. (2014) and Turnell and Shaw (2015) largely corroborate what is observed early on in this experiment.
source: and their findings largely corroborate what we observe early on in our experiment.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings with previous work.

claim: Repeated mating, especially with several different partners, is beneficial for the hatching success of offspring in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Our data reveal that repeated mating, especially with several different partners is beneficial for the hatching success of the offspring.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Self fertilization is detrimental to offspring in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Hence, this could also suggest that self fertilization, as occurred in the No partner treatment, is detrimental to offspring.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of treatments.

claim: Similar negative effects of selfing have been found for many snail species.
source: Similar effects of selfing have been found for many snail species (e.g., Escobar et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The higher number of undeveloped eggs in the No partner treatment corroborates the detrimental effects of selfing.
source: and are corroborated by the higher number of undeveloped eggs in that treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Results so far had not indicated very clear negative effects of selfing for Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Interestingly, results so far had not indicated very clear negative effects of selfing for L. stagnalis (Escobar et al., 2011; Puurtinen et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The observation of negative effects of selfing may reflect that offspring development was looked at in more detail in this study.
source: so the fact that we do observe it here may reflect that we looked at the development of offspring in more detail, or that such effects only become apparent in the long run.
evidence: This is a speculation about why the current study found effects not seen before.

claim: The data are the first to show that multiple mating offers a benefit for the development of eggs of Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Notwithstanding, our data are the first to show that multiple mating does offer a benefit for the development of eggs of L. stagnalis
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The finding that multiple mating benefits egg development is supported by previous work showing that such eggs are heavier.
source: and are supported by previous work that showed that such eggs are heavier (Hoffer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The findings are in line with work on other species showing benefits of multiple mating.
source: These findings are also in line with work on other species (e.g., Callosobruchus maculatus: Power and Holman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to work on another species.

claim: Multiple mating has been shown to preferentially occur with different partners in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Multiple mating has already been shown to preferentially occur with different partners (Koene and Ter Maat, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Behavioural studies imply that Lymnaea stagnalis does not alternate mating roles conditionally.
source: and behavioural studies imply that this species does not alternate mating roles conditionally (i.e., they can swap sexual roles within one mating interaction, but this is not obligatory: Koene and Ter Maat, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The mating mode has implications for whether sexual selection can act independently on the two sexual roles of a hermaphrodite.
source: This is of importance since it has implications for whether sexual selection can act independently on the two sexual roles of a hermaphrodite (Anthes et al., 2010); see also Arnold, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The lack of relation between MSm and MSf supports that the mating mode of Lymnaea stagnalis is unilateral.
source: Given that our current data reveal no relation between MSm and MSf, this supports that the mating mode of this species is unilateral (no exchange of sex roles).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Male and female strategies can probably be optimized independently in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Hence, male and female strategies can probably be optimized independently in this species.
evidence: This is an inference from the unilateral mating mode.

claim: The lack of a clear correlation between RSm and RSf indicates that an individual successful in the male role is not necessarily successful in the female role.
source: The lack of a clear correlation between RSm and RSf also indicates that an individual successful in the male role is not necessarily successful in the female role.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Reproductive success can be gained constantly via the male function, as shown by the significant male sexual selection gradients throughout the experiment.
source: The latter is also supported by our finding that reproductive success can be gained constantly via the male function, as shown by the significant male sexual selection gradients (βmm) throughout the experiment.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: The mating system of Lymnaea stagnalis seems largely male-driven.
source: Given that this mating system seems largely male-driven, we expected to also see cross-sex effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the data on sexual selection gradients.

claim: Cross-sex effects should become visible as negative gradients when looking at male or female reproductive success.
source: These effects should become visible as negative gradients when looking at male or female reproductive success (respectively, βmf or βmPC1 and βfm or βfPC1).
evidence: This is a prediction based on theory.

claim: Negative cross-sex effects emerged more clearly from the PCA approach.
source: Such negative effects emerged more clearly from the PCA approach, and only near the end of the experimental period (βfPC1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The absence of cross-sex effects in earlier studies may be explained by their short duration of several days.
source: This may explain why such cross-sex effects were not found in earlier studies that lasted only for several days (Anthes et al., 2010; Pélissié et al., 2012; Pélissié et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference comparing the current study to previous work.

claim: The results highlight that cross-sex effects do have an impact on the reproductive success of Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Moreover, our results highlight that cross-sex effects do have an impact on the reproductive success of this hermaphroditic animal.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: The observed cross-sex effects can potentially be explained by the reported negative effects of seminal fluid proteins on both sexual functions.
source: The cross-sex effects that we observe can potentially be explained by the reported negative effects of seminal fluid proteins on both sexual functions (Koene et al., 2010; Nakadera et al., 2014b), but this remains to be tested directly.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There was no indication for a trade-off between investing in the two sexes in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Interestingly, we did not find any indication for a trade-off between investing in the two sexes, which would have resulted in a negative βfm (although a trend is seen in the last weeks of the experiment for βfPC1).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Sex allocation theory predicts that increased mating success as a male trades off with female reproductive success, or vice versa.
source: Based on sex allocation theory, one might have expected that increased mating success as a male trades off with female reproductive success (βfm), or vice versa (βmf; Anthes et al., 2010; Charnov, 1979; Schärer, 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citations.

claim: Other studies on different simultaneous hermaphrodites did not find any cross-sex effects.
source: As mentioned above, other studies on different simultaneous hermaphrodites did not find any cross-sex effects, while they did find that the mating system is mainly driven by the male function (B. glabrata: Anthes et al., 2010 and P. acuta: Pélissié et al., 2012, Pélissié et al., 2014; but see Janicke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work supported by citations.

claim: An important difference between previous studies and this study is that while they followed individuals for 3 to 5 days, this study followed them for 56 days.
source: An important difference between those studies and our study is that while they followed individuals for 3 to 5 days, we followed them for 56 days (8 weeks).
evidence: This is a comparison of methodological approaches.

claim: From the start of the experiment, the significant βmm is already captured.
source: Our data showed that from the start, the main effect, the significant βmm, is already captured (also with the PCA approach: βmPC2).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of the data.

claim: The relationship between male mating success and male reproductive success became statistically stronger over time.
source: This relationship became statistically stronger over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of the data.

claim: The negative cross-sex effects only emerged much later into the experiment.
source: In contrast, the negative effects only emerged much later into the experiment, which indicates that such effects on reproductive success may only be detectable in the longer run.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of the data.

claim: Short term experiments only take a snap shot of reproductive success of virgins.
source: Hence, short term experiments only take a snap shot of reproductive success (of virgins).
evidence: This is a methodological insight from comparing the current study to previous work.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis has a unilateral mating system.
source: To conclude, we showed that L. stagnalis has a unilateral mating system
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Sperm donors in Lymnaea stagnalis gain most reproductive success from repeated mating.
source: and that sperm donors gain most reproductive success from repeated mating
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Sperm donors in Lymnaea stagnalis seem to lose some reproductive success in the long run from mating frequently as a female.
source: even though they seem to lose some reproductive success in the long run (a cross-sex effect from mating frequently as a female).
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: Sperm recipients in Lymnaea stagnalis benefit indirectly from repeated mating, since their egg development and hatching success is higher.
source: Our data also do reveal that these sperm recipients benefit indirectly from repeated mating, since their egg development and hatching success is higher.
evidence: This is a summary of a primary finding from the study.

claim: The experimental time frame is very important for the quantification and interpretation of sexual selection measures.
source: Our experiment therefore showed that the experimental time frame is very important for the quantification and interpretation of sexual selection measures, an insight that applies to any mating system with multiple mating.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the study.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis is a species common to the Holarctic region.
source: The basommatophoran pond snail L. stagnalis is a species common to the Holarctic region, and resides in ponds, ditches, and lakes.
evidence: This is background information about the study species.

claim: A laboratory population of Lymnaea stagnalis has been maintained at VU University for more than 50 years.
source: At the mass culture facility at VU University, a laboratory population of L. stagnalis has been maintained on running, low-copper water for more than 50 years (Van Der Steen et al., 1969).
evidence: This is background information about the study population with citation.

claim: At a shell length of about 18 mm, around the age of two months, Lymnaea stagnalis individuals begin to copulate.
source: At a shell length of about 18 mm, around the age of two months, individuals begin to copulate, soon followed by production of egg masses.
evidence: This is background information about the study species.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis has a mixed mating system with high outcrossing rates despite low self-fertilization depression.
source: L. stagnalis has a mixed mating system with high outcrossing rates despite low self-fertilization depression (Nakadera et al., 2014a, Nakadera et al., 2017; Puurtinen et al., 2007; Cain, 1956; Coutellec and Caquet, 2011; Koene et al., 2009).
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by multiple citations.

claim: A single copulation interaction in Lymnaea stagnalis is unilateral.
source: A single copulation interaction is unilateral, meaning that one partner performs the male role and the other the female role.
evidence: This is background information about the study species.

claim: After an initial copulation, role-alternation can take place in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: After an initial copulation role-alternation can take place (Koene and Ter Maat, 2005)
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by citation.

claim: Chain-copulations can be observed in groups of Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: and also chain-copulations can be observed in groups.
evidence: This is background information about the study species.

claim: Mating rates increase with population density in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: Mating rates increase with population density (Koene and Ter Maat, 2007)
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by citation.

claim: Copulation can be easily observed in the laboratory in Lymnaea stagnalis.
source: and copulation can be easily observed in the laboratory (Van Duivenboden and Ter Maat, 1988; De Boer et al., 1996).
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by citations.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis is a promiscuous species.
source: L. stagnalis is a promiscuous species
evidence: This is background information about the study species.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis can store received sperm for about 2 months (62 days).
source: and can store received sperm (allosperm) for about 2 months (62 days: Nakadera et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by citation.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis uses stored sperm seemingly random when fertilizing eggs.
source: and use it seemingly random when fertilizing eggs (Koene et al., 2009).
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by citation.

claim: Lymnaea stagnalis usually lays between 100–300 eggs per week in 1–4 egg masses, depending on mating conditions.
source: Pond snails are highly fecund and usually lay between 100–300 eggs per week in 1–4 egg masses, depending on mating conditions (Hoffer et al., 2012; Van Duivenboden et al., 1985).
evidence: This is background information about the study species supported by citations.

claim: Two hundred immature snails were collected from the mass culture for the experiment.
source: Two hundred immature snails (shell length < 15 mm), that hatched from multiple egg masses laid on the same day (±24 hr), were collected from our mass culture.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: At 14 weeks after hatching, all virgin snails were confirmed to be laying self-fertilized eggs.
source: At 14 weeks after hatching (shell length ~30 mm) all virgins were confirmed to be laying self-fertilized eggs.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and observations.

claim: The quantification of mating success and reproductive success started when animals were 110 days old.
source: The quantification of mating success (MS) and reproductive success (RS) started when animals - still virgin - were 110 days old, at which time they had had plenty of time to fully recover from tissue sampling.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The experiment included three treatments: Multiple partners, Single partner, and No partner.
source: The experiment included three treatments: Multiple partners (25 groups of 5 snails each), Single partner (25 groups of 2 snails each), and No partner (25 single snails that remained virgins).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The focal individual had a microsatellite genotype that could be unequivocally distinguished from the other snails in its group.
source: For the snails in groups, we made sure that the focal had a microsatellite genotype (see Genotyping protocol) that could be unequivocally distinguished from the other snails in its group.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During eight weeks, mating activity was observed twice a week for 7 hr on the first and fourth day of each week.
source: During eight weeks, for each treatment mating activity was observed twice a week for 7 hr on the first and fourth day of each week (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The snails only had access to mating partners during the 7 hr mating trials.
source: The snails only had access to mating partners during these 7 hr mating trials, when they were together in a jar.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Within all groups, copulation and mating role was noted for each individual.
source: Within all groups, copulation and mating role was noted for each individual (175 snails in total all of which mated more than once in the male and female role)
evidence: This describes the experimental design and observations.

claim: Complete observational data was available based on which each individual's mating success could be calculated.
source: hence we had complete observational data based on which we could calculate each individual's MS.
evidence: This describes the data collection.

claim: Cumulative number of matings was used, not mates, because this species mates frequently.
source: We used cumulative number of matings, not mates, because this species mates frequently and within the first weeks all individuals have already mated at least once with each group member in both sexual roles, hence maximizing number of mates.
evidence: This explains the methodological choice.

claim: Due to the restricted number of different mates available, Bateman gradients could not be quantified as these are defined based on mate identity.
source: Thus, due to the restricted number of different mates available, Bateman gradients could not be quantified as these are defined based on mate identity.
evidence: This explains a methodological limitation.

claim: By looking at mating frequency, sexual selection gradients rather than Bateman gradients sensu stricto were determined.
source: By looking at mating frequency we thus determined sexual selection gradients rather than Bateman gradients sensu stricto (see also Anthes et al., 2010; Collet et al., 2014; Fritzsche and Arnqvis, 2013; Marie-Orleach et al., 2016).
evidence: This explains the methodological approach with citations.

claim: The opportunity for selection (I) is defined as the standardized variance in relative reproductive success.
source: This measure is defined as the standardized variance in relative reproductive success and its value is indicative of the opportunity for selection (Gowaty et al., 2003; Jones, 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citations.

claim: The opportunity for sexual selection (Is) is defined as the standardized variance in relative mating success.
source: The opportunity for sexual selection, which is defined as the standardized variance in relative mating success, is captured in the variance measure Is (Arnold, 1994; Anthes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citations.

claim: The sexual selection gradient (β) is the linear least-squares regression slope of sex-specific relative RS on sex-specific relative MS.
source: Such a gradient is the linear least-squares regression slope of sex-specific relative RS on sex-specific relative MS (Jones, 2009; Klug et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by citations.

claim: The sexual selection gradient expresses the expected fitness increase achieved by mating one additional time in a specific sex role.
source: thus expressing the expected fitness increase achieved by mating one additional time in a specific sex role (βm or βf).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the sexual selection gradient measure.
